pos.personaBrief: Queen's Park combined dribbling and passing (Alcock 1878), pinned opponents back (1875 Clydesdale) and kept the ball in close play; no counter-attacking identity.

pro.personaBrief: Close inner dribbling and scientific passing (Robinson, 1876 report) and backing up, with passing on forward in a 2-2-6; not long-ball.

est.personaBrief: Captain Gardner gave position cards and the 2-2-6 had fixed roles, yet play relied on pairs backing each other up and close wing partnerships (Wilson et al., Fraser-Anderson).

lar.personaBrief: 1880s play used wing pairings (Fraser-Anderson, Kay) and wings supplied by centre forwards in 1885; central pair also prominent.

blo.personaBrief: Territorial pressure kept opponents in their own half (1875, 1876 'untiring pertinacity'), six forwards and no deep block; weak evidence for a pressing scheme.

mar.personaBrief: No evidence on marking; two backs and two mobile half-backs facing the opposing forwards suggests loosely individual marking, treated lightly.

pla.personaBrief: A consistent own style under the captain; the one adaptation (three half-backs vs Preston 1886) was reverted as a failure, so identity over adaptation.

res.personaBrief: Amateur club praised for scientific, combined play, with secretaries stressing effort and the game's popularity; style valued, but no defensive game-closing.

sis.personaBrief: Collective combination and fixed positions set by the captain, with pairs supporting each other and small players beating bigger teams as a unit.

jog.personaBrief: Smaller, lighter Scots won on skill and dribbling against heavier English sides (1872 Herald, 1875 report).

bas.personaBrief: Relied on own resources for ten years, tried substitutes before promotion, retained a settled eleven; also chose reputation and experience over youth and recalled veterans.

lid.personaBrief: Captain's power was absolute, he alone picked teams, and the club struck off members who did not respond; equal rules for all, little negotiation.
